strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: using repository commit history as long-term memory for code-localization agents is intuitive, practically relevant, and nicely connected to how human developers build repository expertise.
The method is simple and modular, adding episodic commit retrieval and semantic summaries as tools on top of an existing agentic framework rather than requiring a wholesale redesign.
Evaluation uses relevant benchmarks and strong baselines, especially LocAgent, and reports consistent improvements on SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live.
The paper includes useful ablations for episodic-only and semantic-only memory, plus analyses of per-repository behavior, tool-use shifts, cost tradeoffs, and retrieval choices.
The finding that sparse retrieval outperforms dense retrieval for commit/file-summary memory is interesting and plausible for code-centric entity-heavy queries.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively incremental: the memory mechanisms are straightforward BM25 retrieval over commits and LLM-generated summaries of frequently edited files. The paper’s impact depends heavily on empirical gains rather than a novel algorithmic insight.

The empirical gains, while consistent, are moderate over the strongest baseline: for example, Acc@5 improves from 71.6 to 76.5 on SWE-bench-verified and from 63.1 to 66.2 on SWE-bench-live. This is encouraging but not decisive without statistical significance or variance across runs.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for a top-tier submission. Important implementation choices are underspecified, including prompts for summary generation, the LLM-based tokenizer, linked-issue extraction, overlap filtering, exact retrieval/indexing setup, and whether memory artifacts/code will be released.

Potential leakage and benchmark contamination risks need more rigorous treatment. The paper states that future commits and overlapping linked issues are filtered, but the exact procedure and failure modes are not detailed enough given that historical commits and issues may be closely related to benchmark instances.

The evaluation is limited to file-level localization, not downstream bug fixing or more granular localization. It remains unclear whether the additional memory improves actual patch generation or mainly helps identify broad files.
The SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a filtered subset requiring at most five modified files, which may bias the benchmark toward easier localization cases and reduces confidence in generality.
The method can hurt performance on repositories with limited or irrelevant history, and the paper does not provide a concrete mitigation beyond suggesting future work on deciding when to use memory.
Cost analysis is useful but incomplete: it reports API cost during localization but not the offline cost of constructing summaries, crawling issues, maintaining indexes, or updating memory over time.

The comparison to alternative memory designs is narrow. For example, there is little exploration of commit-patch embeddings, issue-text retrieval, recency weighting, graph-aware memory, or simpler baselines such as directly ranking frequently edited files.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of current repository-level agents: they typically solve each issue without repository-specific historical context.
The proposed memory tools are simple, modular, and easy to integrate into an existing agentic framework such as LocAgent.
The empirical results show consistent Acc@k gains over LocAgent on SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live, with useful ablations separating episodic and semantic memory.
The per-repository and cost analyses are helpful and reveal an important limitation: memory helps most when rich relevant history exists, and can hurt on sparse repositories.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is fairly incremental: BM25 over commit messages/patches plus LLM-generated summaries of frequently edited files. The paper frames this as long-term memory, but the mechanism is closer to retrieval over git history and cached summaries.

The leakage controls are under-specified. The method uses historical commits, linked issues, and patches, but the paper only briefly states that overlapping issues and linked commits are filtered. It does not rigorously define the filtering procedure, similarity thresholds, issue-link resolution, or whether near-duplicate reports and backports are excluded.

The evaluation is limited to file-level localization. The paper does not show that the improved localization translates into better bug fixing, patch generation, or end-to-end SWE-bench resolution, which weakens the claimed practical impact.

The SWE-bench-live subset is filtered to instances requiring five or fewer modified files, but the paper does not justify this choice sufficiently or analyze how it affects difficulty and representativeness.

The gains, while real, are modest over the strongest baseline: 76.5 vs. 71.6 Acc@5 on SWE-bench-verified and 66.2 vs. 63.1 on SWE-bench-live. The paper does not report statistical significance, confidence intervals, or repeated runs for stochastic agent behavior.

The semantic memory design may encode a popularity prior rather than genuine functional understanding; selecting frequently edited files can help because benchmarks are biased toward active files, but the paper does not control against simpler priors such as ranking by edit frequency or bug-fix frequency alone.
The retrieval analysis is narrow, conducted only on django, and does not establish that the chosen memory interface is robust across repositories or issue types.

The paper lacks important reproducibility details: exact prompts for summary generation and agent tool use, retrieval/tokenization implementation, commit/issue crawling details, costs for memory construction, and whether code/data will be released.

Some claims are overstated, especially comparisons to human developer memory and assertions of substantial improvement. The evidence supports a useful retrieval augmentation, but not the broader framing of agents accumulating experience in a human-like way.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: augmenting repository-level coding agents with repository-specific memory from commit history is intuitive, practically relevant, and nicely connected to how human developers build codebase expertise.
The method is simple and modular: episodic memory over prior commits/issues and semantic summaries of active files are easy to integrate into an existing agent such as LocAgent.

Empirical results are encouraging. RepoMem improves over strong baselines on SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live, including a direct gain over LocAgent, with ablations showing that episodic memory is particularly useful and that the combined method performs best.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline accuracy, including per-repository behavior, tool-use shifts, cost tradeoffs, retrieval-method comparison, and a small failure analysis. These make the contribution more credible and informative.
The writing is generally clear, and the figures/examples help explain why historical commits can guide localization.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: the core method is essentially adding BM25 retrieval over commits and LLM-generated summaries as extra tools for an existing localization agent. The paper would be stronger with a deeper algorithmic contribution or a more principled memory-use policy.

The evaluation is limited to file-level localization. Since the motivation is repository-level software engineering and bug fixing, it remains unclear how much the improved localization translates to actual patch generation or issue resolution.

Potential contamination/leakage concerns are only partially addressed. The paper states that commits after the issue base commit and overlapping/linked issues are filtered, but historical commit data can contain related fixes, duplicate reports, backports, or issue references in ways that are difficult to rule out. More rigorous leakage audits would strengthen confidence.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a filtered 130-example subset requiring at most five modified files. This is reasonable for localization, but it narrows the claim and may exclude harder, more realistic multi-file tasks.

The method can hurt performance on repositories with sparse or irrelevant histories, and the current agent lacks a mechanism to decide when memory should be trusted or ignored. This is acknowledged but remains an important practical limitation.

Several implementation details affecting reproducibility are underspecified, including the exact commit/issue crawling procedure, filtering heuristics, prompts for semantic summaries, LLM tokenizer for BM25, cost of offline memory construction, and whether all baselines were rerun under identical settings.

The reported gains, while consistent, are moderate in absolute terms over LocAgent, and the paper does not provide statistical significance or confidence intervals. This matters because SWE-bench subsets can have substantial variance.

strengths: Clear, practically motivated idea: using repository commit history as long-term memory for software engineering agents is intuitive, relevant, and well aligned with how developers build expertise in a codebase.
The method is simple and modular: episodic commit retrieval and semantic summaries of active files are easy to integrate into an existing ReAct-style localization framework such as LocAgent.
Evaluation uses meaningful benchmarks, including SWE-bench-verified and a newer SWE-bench-live subset, and compares against strong retrieval, procedural, and agentic baselines.

The paper provides useful ablations showing that episodic and semantic memory each help, with the full system performing best. The downstream patch-resolution experiment also strengthens the claim that localization gains matter in practice.
The analysis of tool-use shifts, cost tradeoffs, repository-level variation, and sparse versus dense retrieval adds helpful insight beyond a single leaderboard table.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental. The core technical contribution is mostly adding BM25 retrieval over historical commits plus LLM-generated summaries of frequently edited files; this is useful but not especially deep methodologically.

The contamination/leakage controls are underspecified and not fully convincing. Filtering prior commits and overlapping linked issues is a good start, but historical commits, linked issues, duplicate reports, and issue metadata can still contain near-direct hints to ground-truth files or fixes. The paper needs a much more rigorous leakage audit.

The reported gains, while consistent, are modest: +4.9 Acc@5 on SWE-bench-verified and +3.1 on SWE-bench-live over LocAgent, with degradation on low-history repositories. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are reported despite stochastic LLM agents.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a filtered 130-example subset requiring five or fewer modified files, which may overrepresent cases where file-level localization is easier and limits claims about generality.

Evaluation is primarily file-level Acc@k. Since the paper motivates precise code localization, stronger function/class/line-level results would be important, especially because commit history may surface relevant files without demonstrating fine-grained reasoning.

The semantic memory construction is costly and somewhat circular: it uses LocAgent plus GPT-4o to summarize active files, potentially exploring dependencies. The offline cost and implementation complexity are not fully incorporated into comparisons, and the exact prompting/tokenizer details are not sufficiently reproducible.

Fairness of comparison is somewhat unclear. RepoMem gives LocAgent additional repository-evolution information and extra tool calls; stronger controls such as equal-context baselines, commit-message-only retrieval outside the agent, or hotspot-prior baselines would help isolate the value of the proposed agentic memory design.

The paper claims the method emulates human long-term repository memory, but the evidence mainly shows improved retrieval priors from historical metadata. The cognitive framing is plausible but stronger than what the experiments directly establish.

Reproducibility is limited at submission time: source code is only promised upon publication, and several important details about crawling, issue linking, LLM summarization, LLM-based tokenization, and baseline reproduction are missing or relegated to examples.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in repository-level software engineering agents: current localization systems solve each issue from scratch rather than exploiting repository history. The motivation is intuitive and practically meaningful.

The proposed RepoMem interface is simple and easy to understand: episodic memory retrieves prior commits/issues, while semantic memory summarizes frequently edited files. This makes the method modular and straightforward to integrate into LocAgent.

The empirical results show nontrivial improvements over LocAgent on SWE-bench-verified, especially Acc@5 from 71.6 to 76.5, and a smaller improvement on SWE-bench-live from 63.1 to 66.2. The paper also reports a downstream issue-resolution improvement using an Agentless patch-generation pipeline.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the main table, including per-repository breakdowns, tool-use changes, cost comparisons, retrieval-method ablations, and sensitivity to the number of active files in semantic memory.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The main contribution is adding BM25 search over commit messages/patches and LLM summaries of high-churn files as extra tools for an existing agent. This is a plausible engineering extension, but it feels closer to a straightforward retrieval-augmented agent design than a strong top-tier AI contribution.

The evaluation does not rule out simpler baselines. Missing comparisons include using only frequently edited files without LLM summaries, direct BM25 retrieval over files/commit-modified paths, issue-to-commit retrieval without agent integration, adding commit messages as static context, or a simple hotspot prior combined with LocAgent. Without these, it is hard to know whether the gains come from the proposed memory design or from exposing obvious repository-history signals.

There is a serious concern about benchmark leakage or near-leakage. The method explicitly uses historical commits and linked issues, and the paper only says it removes issues with overlapping text and linked commits. This is underspecified and may be insufficient, since related fixes, duplicate reports, backports, nearby commits, release notes, or issue discussions can reveal target files without requiring genuine localization reasoning.

The reported gains are modest and uneven. RepoMem improves SWE-bench-verified Acc@5 by 4.9 points and SWE-bench-live Acc@5 by 3.1 points, but performance drops sharply on repositories with limited history. The method’s applicability therefore depends strongly on repository history quality, which weakens the broad claim that this is a general memory mechanism for agents.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation is small and filtered to 130 examples requiring at most five modified files. This filtering may make localization easier and limits conclusions about harder, more realistic issues. The paper also does not report statistical significance or variance for stochastic LLM-agent runs.

The paper uses a single backbone, GPT-4o, and does not evaluate whether the memory mechanism transfers to weaker, stronger, or open models. Since agent behavior and tool use can be highly model-dependent, this limits the strength of the conclusions.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate. The exact crawling procedure, issue-linking logic, overlap filter, tokenizer prompt, summary-generation prompt, decoding parameters, agent budget, and failure-handling details are not specified enough to reproduce the results. Code is only promised after publication.

The cost analysis is incomplete. The paper reports online tool latency and per-example API costs, but the offline semantic memory cost can be substantial across many repositories, and the main method increases average inference cost on several categories. The claimed efficiency/cost-effectiveness tradeoff is therefore not fully established.

The related-work positioning is thin. The paper discusses software localization, JIT defect prediction, and memory agents, but does not sufficiently engage with simpler historical mining approaches, bug localization using version histories, repository-aware retrieval, or engineering baselines from software maintenance literature.

The conclusions overstate the evidence. The experiments show that repository history can help LocAgent on selected benchmarks, but they do not establish that the agent has acquired human-like long-term memory or that the method robustly improves long-horizon software engineering agents.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important limitation of current software engineering agents: repository-level tasks are typically solved from scratch despite the availability of useful historical repository knowledge.

The proposed RepoMem design is simple, well motivated, and modular. The distinction between episodic memory from past commits/issues and semantic memory from summaries of active files is intuitive and fits the code localization setting well.

The empirical results are convincing enough for a positive assessment: RepoMem improves over strong baselines including LocAgent on SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live, with consistent gains in Acc@1/3/5 and a downstream improvement in issue resolution rate.

The ablations are useful. The paper separately evaluates episodic-only and semantic-only memory, analyzes per-repository behavior, studies retrieval choices, reports cost/latency, and includes sensitivity analysis for the semantic memory size.

The paper is clearly written and well positioned relative to code localization, JIT defect prediction, and memory-enhanced agents. The motivating examples make the value of repository memory concrete.
weaknesses: The main technical contribution is relatively incremental: the method adds BM25-based commit retrieval and LLM-generated file summaries to an existing localization agent, without a substantially new learning algorithm or agent architecture.
The improvements, while meaningful, are moderate. On SWE-bench-live the absolute Acc@5 gain over LocAgent is about 3 points, so the evidence supports usefulness more than a major advance.

The method depends strongly on the quantity and relevance of repository history. The paper itself shows degradation on repositories with limited history, but does not yet provide a robust mechanism for deciding when memory should be ignored.

There remains some risk of benchmark-specific advantage from historical commits and issue links. The authors make reasonable leakage-prevention efforts, but a deeper audit of temporal filtering, linked issue overlap, and similarity to benchmark issues would strengthen confidence.

The evaluation is limited to file-level localization in Python-heavy SWE-bench-style repositories. It is unclear how well the approach transfers to other languages, smaller/private repositories, non-bug tasks, or full autonomous repair beyond the Agentless pipeline experiment.

Reproducibility is mostly described but not fully established in the manuscript, since code and constructed memory resources are promised for release rather than available at review time. Some implementation details of the LLM-based tokenizer and summary generation pipeline could also be specified more precisely.
